27. Combined Quality and Cost Evaluation

 

a. Quality and Cost-Based Selection (QCBS)

 

27.1.In the case of QCBS, the total score is calculated by weighting the technical and financial scores and adding them as per the formula and instructions in the Data Sheet. The Consultant with the Most Advantageous Proposal, which is the Proposal that achieves the highest combined technical and financial scores, will be invited for negotiations.

b. Fixed-Budget Selection (FBS)

27.2In the case of FBS, those Proposals that exceed the budget indicated in ITC 14.1.4 of the Data Sheet shall be rejected.

27.3The Client will select the Consultant with the Most Advantageous Proposal, which is the highest-ranked Technical Proposal that does not exceed the budget indicated in the RFP, and invite such Consultant to negotiate the Contract.

c. Least-Cost Selection

27.4. In the case of Least-Cost Selection (LCS), the Client will select the Consultant with the Most Advantageous Proposal, which is the Proposal with the lowest evaluated total price among those Proposals that achieved the minimum qualifying technical score, and invite such a Consultant to negotiate the Contract.

D.  Negotiations and Award

28. Negotiations

28.1The negotiations will be held at the date and address indicated in the Data Sheet with the Consultant’s representative(s) who must have written power of attorney to negotiate and sign a Contract on behalf of the Consultant.

28.2. The Client shall prepare minutes of negotiations that are signed by the Client and the Consultant’s authorized representative.

a. Availability of Key Experts

28.3.The invited Consultant shall confirm the availability of all Key Experts included in the Proposal as a pre-requisite to the negotiations, or, if applicable, a replacement in accordance with ITC 12. Failure to confirm the Key Experts’ availability may result in the rejection of the Consultant’s Proposal and the Client proceeding to negotiate the Contract with the next-ranked Consultant.

28.4.Notwithstanding the above, the substitution of Key Experts at the negotiations may be considered if due solely to circumstances outside the reasonable control of and not foreseeable by the Consultant, including but not limited to death or medical incapacity. In such case, the Consultant shall offer a substitute Key Expert within the period of time specified in the letter of invitation to negotiate the Contract, who shall have equivalent or better qualifications and experience than the original candidate.

b. Technical Negotiations

28.5.The negotiations include discussions of the Terms of Reference (TORs), the proposed methodology, the Client’s inputs, the special conditions of the Contract, and finalizing the “Description of Services” part of the Contract. These discussions shall not substantially alter the original scope of services under the TOR or the terms of the contract, lest the quality of the final product, its price, or the relevance of the initial evaluation be affected.

c. Financial Negotiations

 

28.6. The negotiations include the clarification of the Consultant’s tax liability in the Client’s country and how it should be reflected in the Contract.

28.7.If the selection method included cost as a factor in the evaluation, the total price stated in the Financial Proposal for a Lump-Sum contract shall not be negotiated.

28.8.In the case of a Time-Based contract, unit rates negotiations shall not take place, except when the offered Key Experts and Non-Key Experts’ remuneration rates are much higher than the typically charged rates by consultants in similar contracts. In such case, the Client may ask for clarifications and, if the fees are very high, ask to change the rates after consultation with the Bank. The format for (i) providing information on remuneration rates in the case of Quality Based Selection; and (ii) clarifying remuneration rates’ structure under this Clause, is provided in Appendix A to the Financial Form FIN-3: Financial Negotiations – Breakdown of Remuneration Rates.

29. Conclusion of Negotiations

29.1. The negotiations are concluded with a review of the finalized draft Contract, which then shall be initialed by the Client and the Consultant’s authorized representative.

29.2.If the negotiations fail, the Client shall inform the Consultant in writing of all pending issues and disagreements and provide a final opportunity to the Consultant to respond. If disagreement persists, the Client shall terminate the negotiations informing the Consultant of the reasons for doing so. After having obtained the Bank’s no objection, the Client will invite the next-ranked Consultant to negotiate a Contract. Once the Client commences negotiations with the next-ranked Consultant, the Client shall not reopen the earlier negotiations.

30. Standstill Period

30.1.The Contract shall not be awarded earlier than the expiry of the Standstill Period. The Standstill Period shall be ten (10) Business Days unless extended in accordance with ITC 33. The Standstill Period commences the day after the date the Client has transmitted to each Consultant (that has not already been notified that it has been unsuccessful) the Notification of Intention to Award the Contract. Where only one Proposal is submitted, or if this contract is in response to an emergency situation recognized by the Bank, the Standstill Period shall not apply.

31.Notification of Intention to Award

31.1.The Client shall send to each Consultant (that has not already been notified that it has been unsuccessful) the Notification of Intention to Award the Contract to the successful Consultant. The Notification of Intention to Award shall contain, at a minimum, the following information:

(a) the name and address of the Consultant with whom the client successfully negotiated a contract;

(b) the contract price of the successful Proposal;

(c) the names of all Consultants included in the short list, indicating those that submitted Proposals;

(d) where the selection method requires, the price offered by each Consultant as read out and as evaluated;

(e) the overall technical scores and scores assigned for each criterion and sub-criterion to each Consultant;

(f) the final combined scores and the final ranking of the Consultants;

(g) a statement of the reason(s) why the recipient’s Proposal was unsuccessful, unless the combined score in above already reveals the reason;

(h)the expiry date of the Standstill Period; and

(i) instructions on how to request a debriefing and/or submit a complaint during the Standstill Period.

32. Notification of Award

32.1.Upon expiry of the Standstill Period, specified in ITC 30.1 or any extension thereof, and upon satisfactorily addressing any complaint that has been filed within the Standstill Period, the Client shall, send a notification of award to the successful Consultant, confirming the Client’s intention to award the Contract to the successful Consultant and requesting the successful Consultant to sign and return the draft negotiated Contract within eight (8) Business Days from the date of receipt of such notification.   The client shall simultaneously request the successful Consultant to submit, within eight (8) Business Days, the Beneficial Ownership Disclosure Form.

Contract Award Notice

Within ten (10) Business Days from the date of notification of award such request, the Client shall publish the Contract Award Notice which shall contain, at a minimum, the following information:

(a) name and address of the Client;

(b) name and reference number of the contract being awarded, and the selection method used;

(c) names of the consultants that submitted proposals, and their proposal prices as read out at financial proposal opening, and as evaluated;

(d) names of all Consultants whose Proposals were rejected or were not evaluated, with the reasons therefor;

(e) the name of the successful consultant, the final total contract price, the contract duration and a summary of its scope; and

(f) successful Consultant’s Beneficial Ownership Disclosure Form, if specified in Data Sheet ITC 32.1.

32.2. The Contract Award Notice shall be published on the Client’s website with free access if available, or in at least one newspaper of national circulation in the Client’s Country, or in the official gazette. The Client shall also publish the contract award notice in UNDB online.

 

33. Debriefing by the Client

33.1. On receipt of the Client’s Notification of Intention to Award referred to in ITC 31.1, an unsuccessful Consultant has three (3) Business Days to make a written request to the Client for a debriefing. The Client shall provide a debriefing to all unsuccessful Consultants whose request is received within this deadline

33.2. Where a request for debriefing is received within the deadline, the Client shall provide a debriefing within five (5) Business Days, unless the Client decides, for justifiable reasons, to provide the debriefing outside this timeframe. In that case, the standstill period shall automatically be extended until five (5) Business Days after such debriefing is provided.  If more than one debriefing is so delayed, the standstill period shall not end earlier than five (5) Business Days after the last debriefing takes place. The Client shall promptly inform, by the quickest means available, all Consultants of the extended standstill period.

33.3. Where a request for debriefing is received by the Client later than the three (3)-Business Day deadline, the Client should provide the debriefing as soon as practicable, and normally no later than fifteen (15) Business Days from the date of publication of Public Notice of Award of contract. Requests for debriefing received outside the three (3)-day deadline shall not lead to extension of the standstill period. 

33.4. Debriefings of unsuccessful Consultants may be done in writing or verbally. The Consultants shall bear their own costs of attending such a debriefing meeting.

 

34. Signing of Contract

34.1.The Contract shall be signed prior to the expiry date of the Proposal validity and promptly after expiry of the Standstill Period, specified in ITC 30.1 or any extension thereof, and upon satisfactorily addressing any complaint that has been filed within the Standstill Period.

Technical Assistance for Development and Implementation of “First Steps Forward” Plans and Capacity Building for Scale

 

             I.   BACKGROUND

The Government of Ukraine is implementing a comprehensive reform of the education sector aimed at strengthening teaching and learning conditions and enhancing management capacities across all levels of education, which is one of the key tasks on the path of Ukraine's accession to the EU. With the adoption in 2024 of the new Law of Ukraine "On Preschool Education", which entered into force on January 1, 2025, active transformation processes have also covered preschool education.

Early childhood and preschool education ranks first among the strategic priorities identified by the Strategic Action Plan of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine until 2027, approved by the Order of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine dated March 7, 2024 No. 276. The ultimate goal of the reform is to ensure access to quality preschool education for every child, including children with special educational needs, which is planned to be achieved through a number of the following strategic goals: accessibility, highly qualified and motivated staff, compliance of the quality and content of education with European requirements, the functioning of effective systems for monitoring and assessing quality, management and financing.

The European Commission's Communication on the EU's Enlargement Policy for 2024 notes the steps taken as achieving some progress. It emphasizes the next task of ensuring the implementation of the legislation on preschool education, which puts in place measures aligning to EU principles and focuses on high-quality early childhood education, guaranteeing access for children of early and preschool age, fair rules for the functioning of preschool entities, and decent working conditions for employees.

Implementation of this reform is also accompanied by the development of the draft Strategy for preschool education development presented during the event “First Steps Forward”, new secondary legislation, and additional budget allocations.

These reforms, which are the most transformative in more than three decades, will be implemented in two phases. The first phase involves developing capacity at the national and local levels for implementation of reforms on a limited scale, approximately 35 territorial communities (hromadas), combined with a rigorous process evaluation to prepare for scale up. The second phase involves implementation of the Strategy at the national level.

In 2024, Ukraine, together with the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association (hereinafter referred to as the World Bank), signed the agreements for the Operation “Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine” (hereinafter referred to as LEARN or the Operation).

LEARN was designed to address critical challenges and provide the necessary support to the education sector in accordance with the Strategic Action Plan of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine until 2027, approved by Order of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine dated 07.03.2024 No. 276 (hereinafter referred to as the Strategic Plan).

The Operation focuses on supporting the priorities “1. Early Childhood and Preschool Education” and “2. Reform of the New Ukrainian School” stipulated in the Strategic Plan.

To support the first stage of the preschool education reform, the Government requested additional resources under the Technical Assistance component of the LEARN Operation.

The LEARN objectives are: (i) to improve teaching and learning conditions; and (ii) to strengthen the management capacity of the education system. The total LEARN financing amounts to US$737 mln  provides a combination of the World Bank financing instruments: Program for Results (PforR) – US$ 675.9 mln and Investment Project Financing (IPF) – US$61.1 mln.

The Program-for-Results (PforR) is implemented through a US$235 million loan provided by Bank resources, supported by loan enhancement from the Advancing Needed Credit Enhancement for Ukraine (ADVANCE Ukraine) Trust Fund, which is backed by the Government of Japan. This is formalized under the Loan Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development for the Program (LOAN No 9721-UA). An additional US$150 million is provided under the Special Program for Ukraine and Moldova Recovery (SPUR) of the International Development Association (IDA) Crisis Facility, as outlined in the Financing Agreement between Ukraine and the International Development Association for the Program (CREDIT No 7626-UA). On July 1, 2025, the Financing Agreement (Additional Financing: Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program) between Ukraine and the International Development Association (CREDIT No 7905-UA) was signed in the amount of US$4.9 million.On June 9, 2026, a Loan Agreement (Third Additional Financing for Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program) was signed between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (Loan No. K019-UA) in the amount of $286 million.

Furthermore, US$30 million in Investment Project Financing (IPF) is secured under the Grant Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, acting as the administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (URTF GRANT No TF0C5794). On December 19, 2025, the Grant Agreement (Additional Financing for Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Project) between UKRAINE and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association jointly acting as a Supervising Entity for the Global Partnership for Education Fund and as administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (GPE GRANT No TF0D0613, URTF GRANT No TF0D0612) was signed in the amount of US$31.1 million.

The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine has established the Early Childhood Education Development Office (ECEDO). Functioning as a technical implementation office within the ministry, ECEDO provides operational and expert support to coordinate overall reform efforts across several areas, including access and financing, content of education and teacher professional development, inclusion, quality assurance, legal and regulatory frameworks, as well as intersectoral cooperation. The office will also be responsible for monitoring the implementation of reforms in the field of Early Childhood and Preschool Education (ECPE). The establishment of ECEDO strengthens the capacity of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine to manage donor-funded technical assistance, provide support to participating communities, ensure coherence between reform components, and integrate project results into national systems for long-term sustainability and scalability.

The ECEDO brings together multidisciplinary teams of experts organized across three technical pillars — Access and Financing, Content and Teacher Professional Development, Inclusion complemented by cross-sectoral experts in QualityAssurance, Legal and Normative Support, Social and Behavior Change (SBC) and Communication, and Physical and Learning Spaces (PLS).

On this basis, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine intends to engage a qualified Consultant to design and deliver a comprehensive training and support program for hromadas on the Training Program on Implementing Preschool Education Reform and Adjusting and/or Developing Draft Local Targeted and Budget Programs for Early Childhood Education  in Hromadas The program will follow a phased approach combining content development, pilot implementation, scaling, and institutionalization of training tools and methodologies.

Under Component A, the focus will be on the development and implementation of a structured training program for hromadas.The training program will target key representatives of local self-government bodies involved in planning, financing, management, and implementation of ECPE reform at the local level, including: Deputy Head of the Hromada; Director of the Education Department or Head of the Education Unit; Deputy Director of the Education Department responsible for preschool education; Head of the Preschool Education Unit; representative of the hromada financial unit responsible for the education budget; Head of the Financial and Economic Unit of the Education Department / Chief Accountant; Director of a preschool education institution (as a representative of the practical implementation level); and, where relevant, representative of the Department of Economy or Strategic Development. The content and structure of the training program will be tailored to the functional responsibilities and capacity gaps of these target groups, taking into account their specific educational and professional development needs related to ECPE reform implementation. This includes strengthening competencies in system analysis and supply-demand assessment, stakeholder engagement and behavior change, financial planning and network configuration, application of the normative framework, quality assurance and monitoring, as well as practical use of tools, templates, and data-informed decision-making approaches. The training program will be modular competency-based and oriented towards practical application, using materials provided by the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and incorporating applied learning methodologies, case studies, and hands-on exercises to support the development of sustainable local ECPE solutions and local targeted and budget ECE programs.  Local targeted and budget ECE programs will define a three-year implementation pathway for optimizing ECPE networks, introducing flexible service delivery models, ensuring financial sustainability, and embedding mechanisms for continuous quality improvement. 

Following the training development, the consultant  will create a blended learning program to approximately 35 hromadas, engaging around 250 representatives. The training will combine online modules with in-person sessions delivered in cohort format and will be strongly practice-oriented, utilizing real hromada data and focusing on analytical, financial, and planning exercises. Structured mentoring and technical assistance will be provided to participating hromadas throughout the full period of adjustment and/or development of local targeted and budget ECE programs and for three months after the final day of in-person training delivery. This support will ensure that hromada teams are able to apply the  methodology delivered in their everyday work practice, use local data, conduct financial and network planning, and prepare evidence-based, costed, inclusive, and operationally feasible local targeted and budget ECE programs.

The core training content will be based on  a structured methodology for the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs which will be designed, taught and applied for development of local documents. This methodology will include comprehensive supply and demand analysis(including public and private provision of ECPE services), demographic projections, network efficiency assessments, the development of alternative network configuration scenarios, financial modelling, and the integration of inclusion considerations. Particular attention will be given to stakeholder consultation processes, prioritization of implementation actions, and risk management.

The final stage of this phase will include a structured evaluation of training effectiveness, usability of tools, and the quality of adjusted and/or developed local targeted and budget ECE programs. The results of this evaluation will inform the refinement of the training package, tools and templates, and MEL approaches, thereby establishing a strong foundation for scaling.

Component B will focus on institutionalization and scaling of the developed approaches at the national level. This will include the development of a comprehensive LMS-based course for the hromada representatives reflecting the full structure of the self-paced training program. The course will include interactive elements, instructional materials, video content, and practical tools.

Quality assurance shall be embedded across all components of the Assignment and reflected in the relevant deliverables under Component A, Component B, and Component C. The Consultant shall apply practical tools for reviewing the quality of training materials, training delivery, mentoring support, LMS-based learning, and developed local targeted and budget ECE programs.

The Consultant shall also collect and analyze feedback, document lessons learned, and use these findings to improve training content, mentoring support, LMS materials, and recommendations for scale-up, in alignment with existing project monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.

The activities shall be implemented within the 13 month period.

II.  OBJECTIVE

The objective of this assignment is to support the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine (MoES) through the engagement of a qualified Consultant to design, deliver, and support the implementation of a comprehensive capacity-building program for hromadas on the adjustment and/or development of local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Specifically, the Consultant shall:

a) to design a structured guidelines for the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs;

b) to develop and deliver a structured training program in a blended format to approximately 250 representatives from 35 hromadas;

c) to provide technical assistance and mentoring to hromadas selected by MoES in the development, submission, and approval of approximately 35 local targeted and budget ECE programs, including peer-learning, inter-hromada dialogue, study tours, and exchange visits. Support shall be provided throughout the preparation period and for three months after the final day of in-person training delivery. Study tours shall cover approximately -70 participants in groups of 20 participants, with an estimated 3-4  study tours conducted depending on logistics and group composition;

d) to prepare the evaluation report on training effectiveness and the quality of developed local targeted and budget ECE programs;

e) to develop and launch LMS course based on the refined 5-module training program for local government bodies.

f) to develop a coherent approach to ensuring the quality of the training program and LMS course, aligned with existing project monitoring and evaluation mechanisms; to prepare practical tools for reviewing the quality of training content, curriculum, TLM, LMS materials and implementation; to assess the quality of hromada-level ECE programs/plans and implementation readiness; and to collaborate with the third-party monitoring and evaluation agency to ensure coherence, avoid duplication, and support evidence-based decision-making during implementation. 

 

III. SCOPE OF SERVICES

Component A. Development and Pilot Implementation of the Training Program in Hromadas

A.1. To design structured guidance for the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs.

 

The Consultant shall design and apply a structured guidance for development of local targeted and budget ECE programs. Given the analytical and research-oriented nature of this assignment, the Consultant shall ensure the methodological quality and practical applicability of the approach, including through the use of relevant data sources, evidence-based analytical tools, and expert validation procedures. The final guidance shall be submitted to the MoES for review and approval before being used for training delivery  in hromadas.

 

The guidance for the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs shall include:

  1. supply and demand analysis (including both public and private provision of early childhood and preschool education services;
  2. demographic projections;
  3. network efficiency assessment;
  4. workforce planning, including staffing needs and training requirements for the ECPE workforce;
  5. strengthening data systems and analytical capacity for ECPE planning and financing, including the ability of hromadas to accurately track enrolled and unenrolled children, attendance, SEN, and transportation needs;
  6. financial modelling and costing (development of 2–3 network configuration scenarios, including cost-per-child and medium-term budget projections under different network configuration scenarios);
  7. selection of a preferred scenario;
  8. inclusion and SEN considerations;
  9. stakeholder consultation processes (including parents);
  10. implementation sequencing and prioritization;
  11. risk analysis and mitigation.

Key Deliverable:

1.Plan for ensuring the quality of  educational activity, covering both development (including development of the training content (guidance for the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs), training curriculum and TLM) and implementation of the training program.

2. Guidance on the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs approved by MoES.

A.2. To develop a structured training program  for approximately 250 representatives from 35 hromadas and guidance for training delivery to hromadas.

The Consultant shall develop, utilizing materials provided by MOES (but not limited to), a structured training program of at least 2.5 ECTS credits (based on the proposed structure, goals and expected learning outcomes presented in Annex 1) in a blended format for approximately 250 representatives from 35 hromadas. The program should consist of five core modules and 1 preparatory on-line module, tailored to the ECPE reform context and directly linked to the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Modules shall cover at minimum:

1.Data-driven management

Analysis of the network (including public and private provision of ECPE services), demographic trends, financial indicators, and population projections; assessment of efficiency and identification of optimization opportunities.

2.Financial model and budget efficiency

Calculation of the cost of service per child, scenario modelling, assessment of the financial effect, and creation of fiscal space through the release and reinvestment of resources, as well as workforce planning within the network, including staffing needs and training requirements.

3.Implementation of the Law of Ukraine “On Preschool Education”

Network configuration, introduction of new types of preschool education institutions, and outsourcing of non-core functions.

4.Change management and implementation

Development of a roadmap, definition of KPIs, risk management, change management approach, and communication of decisions.

5.Quality of preschool education and its monitoring

Assessment of the impact of decisions on the quality of and access to services; identification of priorities for reinvestment of resources; introduction of approaches to regular quality monitoring at the hromada level.

The Consultant shall propose:

  1. a detailed curriculum based on the framework requirements (Annex 1) and training and learning materials (TLM) for preparatory online learning modules and in-person sessions;
  2. practical tools and templates;
  3. applied learning approaches (case-based, problem-solving).

The modular training program will target local representatives of the “change teams” established within participating hromadas. The “change team” is a team composed of approximately 6–8 representatives of the hromada, depending on the size of the hromada and may include, but are not limited to, representatives of hromada leadership, education departments, preschool education units, financial and economic units, preschool education institutions, and departments responsible for economy or strategic development. The exact composition of each hromada team may vary depending on the local governance structure and distribution of responsibilities for ECPE planning, budgeting, and implementation. 

An indicative list of possible target group representatives is provided below.

 

  1. Deputy Head of the Hromada;
  2. Director of the Department / Head of the Education Department;
  3. Deputy Director of the Education Department (responsible for preschool education);
  4. Head of the Preschool Education Unit;
  5. Representative of the Hromada Financial Unit (responsible for the education budget);

  8. Representative of the Department of Economy / Strategic Development;

    4. national-scale deployment.

Annex1

Framework Requirements for the Training Program on Implementing Preschool Education Reform and Developing local targeted and budget ECE programs in Hromadas

Overall Logic

The training program is designed as a modular, competency-based learning pathway aimed at strengthening the capacity representatives of local self-government bodies and other hromada-level education stakeholders involved in the planning, financing, management, and implementation Early Childhood and Preschool Education and Care (ECPEC) reform implementation at the local level.

The program combines practical analytical tools, policy implementation guidance, financial planning methodologies, and participatory approaches, templates, and real hromada data  to support the development of evidence-based and operationally feasible local targeted and budget ECE programs. It is strongly practice-oriented and focuses on the practical application of analytical approaches, tools, and templates required for effective ECPEC reform implementation.

The modular structure covers key thematic areas, including ECPEC system analysis and supply-demand assessment (including public and private provision of ECPE services) , stakeholder engagement and behavior change communication, financial planning and network configuration, application of the normative framework, and quality evaluation and monitoring.

The learning approach integrates in-person practice-oriented workshops, online/self-paced learning, mentoring and coaching support, practical assignments based on real hromada data, peer learning, and case studies. Special attention is given to inclusion, participatory governance, evidence-based decision-making, and sustainable local planning approaches as cross-cutting principles across all modules.

Upon successful completion of the training program and fulfillment of the applicable assessment and participation requirements, participants shall receive certificates confirming completion of the professional development program.

Module Descriptions

Module 0. preparatory on - line

Module Objective

This preparatory online module is designed to ensure that participating hromadas are ready for the in-person training sessions and can engage in practical, data-informed work on the development of their local targeted and budget ECE programs.

The module focuses on introducing participants to the overall logic, objectives, structure, and expected outputs of the training program. It also guides hromada teams in identifying, collecting, organizing, and submitting the key materials, data, and documents required for further analysis during the in-person sessions. These may include information on the existing ECPEC network, demographic trends, enrollment and coverage data, infrastructure and staffing, budget and expenditure data, existing local programs, and relevant strategic or planning documents.

The purpose of the module is to ensure that, by the time hromada teams gather for the in-person training, they have already completed the preparatory work and can focus on the practical development of evidence-based, costed, inclusive, and operationally feasible local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Understand the overall purpose, structure, and expected results of the training program.
  2. Understand the role of local targeted and budget ECE programs in implementing ECPEC reform at the hromada level.
  3. Identify the key types of data, materials, and documents required for local ECPEC planning.
  4. Collect and organize baseline information on the existing ECPEC network, service coverage, infrastructure, staffing, and financial resources.
  5. Compile relevant local strategic, budgetary, regulatory, and planning documents for further analysis.
  6. Conduct a preliminary review of available hromada-level data and identify information gaps.
  7. Prepare materials and initial inputs needed for practical work during the in-person training sessions.
  8. Understand how collected data and documents will be used during the development of local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Key Terms

Preparatory online learning; baseline data collection; hromada profile; ECPEC network data; enrollment data; demographic data; budget data; local planning documents; local targeted and budget ECE programs; data readiness; document review; information gaps; training preparation; evidence-based planning; practical assignments; hromada-level analysis.

Module 1. Data-driven management

Module Objective

This module introduces participants to approaches and tools for comprehensive analysis of the local ECPEC system, including analysis of the network (public and private provision of ECPE services), demographic trends, financial indicators, and population projections, as well as assessment of current and projected supply and demand for preschool education services. Participants will learn how to use demographic, financial, infrastructural, and enrollment data to support evidence-based planning and decision-making at the hromada level.

The module focuses on assessing the efficiency of the ECPEC network,  identifying access gaps, inefficiencies, underserved populations, and opportunities for optimization and diversification of ECPEC services. Participants will also explore approaches to scenario planning and preparation of analytical inputs for local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Understand the structure and functioning of the local ECPEC system.
  2. Conduct supply and demand assessments using demographic and administrative data.
  3. Analyze the local ECPEC network (public and private provision of ECPE services ), demographic trends, financial indicators, and population projections.
  4. Analyze enrollment trends, service coverage, and accessibility gaps.
  5. Assess network efficiency and identify opportunities for optimization.
  6. Identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks within the ECPEC network.
  7. Use analytical tools to support evidence-based planning and forecasting.
  8. Develop alternative scenarios for network optimization and service diversification.
  9. Integrate inclusion and equity considerations into system analysis.

Key Terms

Supply-demand assessment; demographic (population) projections; ECPEC network; enrollment trends;financial indicators; accessibility; service coverage; network efficiency; network optimization; diversification of services; evidence-based planning; data analysis; forecasting; underserved groups; inclusion; local planning.

Module 2. Financial model and budget efficiency 

Module Objective

 

This module introduces participants to financial planning methodologies and tools required for development of sustainable and costed local targeted and budget ECE programs.

Participants will learn approaches to budgeting, costing, financial modeling, and network configuration, including preparation of alternative service delivery scenarios and optimization models. The module emphasizes practical application of financial tools using real hromada data and focuses on balancing quality, accessibility, efficiency, and sustainability of ECPEC services.The module also covers calculation of the cost of service per child, scenario modelling, assessment of the financial effect of proposed options, and creation of fiscal space through the release and reinvestment of resources. In addition, participants will consider workforce planning within the network, including staffing needs and training requirements.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Understand principles of financial planning in ECPEC.
  2. Conduct costing and financial analysis for preschool education services, including calculation of the cost of service per child.
  3. Develop and compare alternative network configuration scenarios, including scenario modelling and assessment of their financial effect.
  4. Use financial modelling tools for planning and forecasting.
  5. Analyze operational efficiency and sustainability of service delivery models, including opportunities to create fiscal space through release and reinvestment of resources.
  6. Prepare evidence-based and costed local targeted and budget ECE programs.
  7. Integrate inclusion and accessibility considerations into financial planning.
  8. Assess financial risks and mitigation measures.
  9. Plan workforce needs within the preschool education network, including staffing needs and training requirements.

Key Terms

Financial planning; costing; budgeting; financial modelling; network configuration; operational efficiency; sustainability; expenditure analysis; forecasting; alternative scenarios; service delivery models; optimization; local targeted and budget ECE programs; risk management; inclusion financing; cost of service per child; scenario modelling; financial effect assessment; fiscal space; release and reinvestment of resources; workforce planning; staffing needs; training requirements.

Module 3. Implementation of the Law of Ukraine “On Preschool Education”

Module Objective

This module introduces participants to the legal, policy, and normative framework governing Early Childhood and Preschool Education and Care in Ukraine.

Participants will explore the New Law of Ukraine on Preschool Education, relevant regulations, standards, and implementation procedures that define the responsibilities of local authorities and education stakeholders. The module aims to strengthen participants’ ability to apply normative requirements in planning, management, financing, and service delivery processes, including network configuration, introduction of new types of preschool education institutions, and outsourcing of non-core functions.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Understand the structure of the national ECPEC normative framework.
  2. Apply the Law of Ukraine on Preschool Education and related regulations.
  3. Identify responsibilities of local self-government bodies within ECPEC reform implementation.
  4. Apply legal and regulatory requirements in local planning and budgeting processes.
  5. Ensure compliance with standards related to access, quality, inclusion, and governance.
  6. Use normative documents to support development of local policies and procedures.
  7. Navigate institutional roles and intersectoral coordination mechanisms.
  8. Apply normative requirements related to network configuration and the introduction of new types of preschool education institutions.
  9. Understand legal and regulatory conditions for outsourcing non-core functions in ECPEC service delivery.

Key Terms

Normative framework; Law on Preschool Education; regulations; standards; governance; local self-government; institutional responsibilities; compliance; implementation procedures; policy framework; decentralization; intersectoral coordination; inclusion standards; network configuration; new types of preschool education institutions; outsourcing; non-core functions.

Module 4. Change management and implementation

Module Objective

This module introduces participants to principles and practical approaches for stakeholder engagement, participatory governance, and behavior change communication in the context of ECPEC reform implementation.

Participants will explore methods for engaging parents, educators, local authorities, community leaders, and other stakeholders in planning and decision-making processes. Particular attention is devoted to building public trust, overcoming resistance to reform, promoting inclusive participation, and strengthening communication strategies that support positive behavioral and social change. The module also covers development of a reform implementation roadmap, definition of key performance indicators (KPIs), risk management, change management approaches, and effective communication of decisions to stakeholders and the wider community.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Identify key stakeholders involved in ECPEC reform implementation.
  2. Analyze stakeholder interests, influence, and engagement needs.
  3. Develop stakeholder engagement and communication plans.
  4. Apply participatory approaches in local planning and consultation processes.
  5. Use behavior change communication techniques to support reform implementation.
  6. Facilitate dialogue and consensus-building among stakeholders.
  7. Address resistance and manage sensitive communication situations.
  8. Promote inclusive and transparent communication practices.
  9. Develop a roadmap for ECPEC reform implementation at the local level.
  10. Define KPIs to monitor progress and support evidence-based decision-making.
  11. Apply risk management and change management approaches in stakeholder engagement and reform implementation.
  12. Communicate decisions clearly and transparently to stakeholders and communities.

Key Terms

Stakeholder engagement; participatory governance; consultation; behavior change communication; public awareness; advocacy; communication strategy; social mobilization; community participation; consensus-building; transparency; inclusion; trust-building; risk communication, roadmap; key performance indicators; KPIs; risk management; change management; communication of decisions.

Module 5. Quality of preschool education and its monitoring

Module Objective

This module introduces participants to approaches and tools for monitoring, evaluation, accountability, and learning (MEAL) in the ECPEC sector both on the policy implementation and educational system and institutions levels in close integration with the quality assurance provisions.

Participants will explore the quality assurance framework for early childhood education and educational activities, systems and indicators used to assess implementation readiness, effectiveness of local programs, and progress of ECPEC reform. The module emphasizes practical use of monitoring tools, data systems, feedback mechanisms, and evidence-based decision-making approaches. The module also covers assessment of the impact of decisions on the quality of and access to services, identification of priorities for reinvestment of resources, and introduction of approaches to regular quality monitoring at the hromada level.

Special attention is devoted to developing local monitoring systems that support continuous improvement, accountability, and sustainability.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this module, participants will be able to:

  1. Understand principles of monitoring, evaluation, accountability, and learning in ECPEC and quality assurance framework.
  2. Use quality indicators and monitoring tools to assess implementation progress.
  3. Conduct monitoring of local targeted and budget ECE programs and service delivery quality.
  4. Analyze and interpret monitoring data for decision-making.
  5. Develop local monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
  6. Apply feedback and learning approaches for continuous improvement.
  7. Support evidence-based management and accountability practices.
  8. Integrate inclusion and equity indicators into monitoring systems.
  9. Assess the impact of local decisions on the quality of and access to ECPEC services.
  10. Identify priorities for reinvestment of resources based on monitoring data and evidence.
  11. Introduce approaches to regular quality monitoring at the hromada level.

Key Terms

Monitoring and evaluation; MEL framework; quality assurance; indicators; accountability; reporting; evidence-based decision-making; implementation readiness; continuous improvement; feedback loops; data systems; performance tracking; quality monitoring; inclusion indicators, impact assessment; access to services; service quality; reinvestment priorities; resource reinvestment; regular quality monitoring; hromada-level monitoring .

  1. Force Majeure
 

a.      Definition

    1. For the purposes of this Contract, “Force Majeure” means an event which is beyond the reasonable control of a Party, is not foreseeable, is unavoidable, and makes a Party’s performance of its obligations hereunder impossible or so impractical as reasonably to be considered impossible under the circumstances, and subject to those requirements, includes, but is not limited to, war, riots, civil disorder, earthquake, fire, explosion, storm, flood or other adverse weather conditions, strikes, lockouts or other industrial action confiscation or any other action by Government agencies.
    2. Force Majeure shall not include (i) any event which is caused by the negligence or intentional action of a Party or such Party’s Experts, Sub-consultants or agents or employees, nor (ii) any event which a diligent Party could reasonably have been expected to both take into account at the time of the conclusion of this Contract, and avoid or overcome in the carrying out of its obligations hereunder.
    3. Force Majeure shall not include insufficiency of funds or failure to make any payment required hereunder.

b.      No Breach of Contract

    1. The failure of a Party to fulfill any of its obligations hereunder shall not be considered to be a breach of, or default under, this Contract insofar as such inability arises from an event of Force Majeure, provided that the Party affected by such an event has taken all reasonable precautions, due care and reasonable alternative measures, all with the objective of carrying out the terms and conditions of this Contract.

c.      Measures to be Taken

    1. A Party affected by an event of Force Majeure shall continue to perform its obligations under the Contract as far as is reasonably practical, and shall take all reasonable measures to minimize the consequences of any event of Force Majeure.
    2. A Party affected by an event of Force Majeure shall notify the other Party of such event as soon as possible, and in any case not later than fourteen (14) calendar days following the occurrence of such event, providing evidence of the nature and cause of such event, and shall similarly give written notice of the restoration of normal conditions as soon as possible.
    3. Any period within which a Party shall, pursuant to this Contract, complete any action or task, shall be extended for a period equal to the time during which such Party was unable to perform such action as a result of Force Majeure.
    4. During the period of their inability to perform the Services as a result of an event of Force Majeure, the Consultant, upon instructions by the Client, shall either:

(a)    demobilize, in which case the Consultant shall be reimbursed for additional costs they reasonably and necessarily incurred, and, if required by the Client, in reactivating the Services; or

(b)    continue with the Services to the extent reasonably possible, in which case the Consultant shall continue to be paid under the terms of this Contract and be reimbursed for additional costs reasonably and necessarily incurred.

    1. In the case of disagreement between the Parties as to the existence or extent of Force Majeure, the matter shall be settled according to Clauses GCC 49 & 50.
  1. Suspension

  1. Forced Labor
    1. The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage forced labor. Forced labor consists of any work or service, not voluntarily performed, that is exacted from an individual under threat of force or penalty, and includes any kind of involuntary or compulsory labor, such as indentured labor, bonded labor or similar labor-contracting arrangements.

No persons shall be employed or engaged who have been subject to trafficking. Trafficking in persons is defined as the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harboring or receipt of persons by means of the threat or use of force or other forms of coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power, or of a position of vulnerability, or of the giving or receiving of payments or benefits to achieve the consent of a person having control over another person, for the purposes of exploitation.

  1. Child Labor
    1. The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage a child under the age of 14 unless the national law specifies a higher age (the minimum age).

The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage a child between the minimum age and the age of 18 in a manner that is likely to be hazardous, or to interfere with, the child’s education, or to be harmful to the child’s health or physical, mental, spiritual, moral, or social development.

The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall only employ or engage children between the minimum age and the age of 18 after an appropriate risk assessment has been conducted by the Consultant with the Client’s consent. The Consultant shall be subject to regular monitoring by the Client that includes monitoring of health, working conditions and hours of work.

Work considered hazardous for children is work that, by its nature or the circumstances in which it is carried out, is likely to jeopardize the health, safety, or morals of children. Such work activities prohibited for children include work:

  1. with exposure to physical, psychological or sexual abuse;
  2. underground, underwater, working at heights or in confined spaces;
  3. with dangerous machinery, equipment or tools, or involving handling or transport of heavy loads;
  4. in unhealthy environments exposing children to hazardous substances, agents, or processes, or to temperatures, noise or vibration damaging to health; or
  5. under difficult conditions such as work for long hours, during the night or in confinement on the premises of the employer.

  1. Purpose
    1. The Bank’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines and this annex apply with respect to procurement under Bank Investment Project Financing operations.
  2. Requirements
  1. The Bank requires that Borrowers (including beneficiaries of Bank financing); bidders (applicants/proposers), consultants, contractors and suppliers; any sub-contractors, sub-consultants, service providers or suppliers; any agents (whether declared or not); and any of their personnel, observe the highest standard of ethics during the procurement process, selection and contract execution of Bank-financed contracts, and refrain from Fraud and Corruption.
  2. To this end, the Bank:
  1. Defines, for the purposes of this provision, the terms set forth below as follows:
  1. “corrupt practice” is the offering, giving, receiving, or soliciting, directly or indirectly, of anything of value to influence improperly the actions of another party;
  2. “fraudulent practice” is any act or omission, including misrepresentation, that knowingly or recklessly misleads, or attempts to mislead, a party to obtain financial or other benefit or to avoid an obligation;
  3. “collusive practice” is an arrangement between two or more parties designed to achieve an improper purpose, including to influence improperly the actions of another party;
  4. “coercive practice” is impairing or harming, or threatening to impair or harm, directly or indirectly, any party or the property of the party to influence improperly the actions of a party;
  5. “obstructive practice” is:
  1. deliberately destroying, falsifying, altering, or concealing of evidence material to the investigation or making false statements to investigators in order to materially impede a Bank investigation into allegations of a corrupt, fraudulent, coercive, or collusive practice; and/or threatening, harassing, or intimidating any party to prevent it from disclosing its knowledge of matters relevant to the investigation or from pursuing the investigation; or
  2. acts intended to materially impede the exercise of the Bank’s inspection and audit rights provided for under paragraph 2.2 e. below.
  1. Rejects a proposal for award if the Bank determines that the firm or individual recommended for award, any of its personnel, or its agents, or its sub-consultants, sub-contractors, service providers, suppliers and/ or their employees, has, directly or indirectly, engaged in corrupt, fraudulent, collusive, coercive, or obstructive practices in competing for the contract in question;
  2. In addition to the legal remedies set out in the relevant Legal Agreement, may take other appropriate actions, including declaring misprocurement, if the Bank determines at any time that representatives of the Borrower or of a recipient of any part of the proceeds of the loan engaged in corrupt, fraudulent, collusive, coercive, or obstructive practices during the procurement process, selection and/or execution of the contract in question,  without the Borrower having taken timely and appropriate action satisfactory to the Bank to address such practices when they occur, including by failing to inform the Bank in a timely manner at the time  they knew of the practices;
  3. Pursuant to the Bank’s Anti- Corruption Guidelines and in accordance with the Bank’s prevailing sanctions policies and procedures, may sanction a firm or individual, either indefinitely or for a stated period of time, including by publicly declaring such firm or individual ineligible (i) to be awarded or otherwise benefit from a Bank-financed contract, financially or in any other manner;[1] (ii) to be a nominated[2] sub-contractor, consultant, manufacturer or supplier, or service provider of an otherwise eligible firm being awarded a Bank-financed contract; and (iii) to receive the proceeds of any loan made by the Bank or otherwise to participate further in the preparation or implementation of any Bank-financed project;

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSION OF INTEREST

 

 

Country:  MOZAMBIQUE

Project:  Mphanda Nkuwa Hydroelectric Project

Agreement: Preparation Advance No. -V522-MZ.

Assignment Title: Individual Consultancy Services to Provision Hydrologist Specialist Project Advisor for providing Project Advisory to undertaking the review of the hydrological studies of the planned Mphanda Nkuwa Hydropower Project.

 

Reference: MZ-GMNK-442364-CS-INDV

 

 

 

The Government of Mozambique (GoM) hereinafter referred to as “the Borrower” have received Advance funds from International Development Association (IDA) towards the costs of the Mphanda Nkuwa Hydroelectric Project, Preparation Phase. The funds have been channeled through the Mphanda Nkuwa Hydroelectric Project Office (GMNK) as the Project Implementation Agency, and GMNK intends to apply part of the proceeds for Consulting Services for providing Project Advisory for undertaking the review of the hydrological studies of the planned Mphanda Nkuwa Hydropower Project.

 

 

The GMNK now invites eligible Individual Consultant (“Consultants”) to express their interest in providing the Services. Interested Individual Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the services. The shortlisting criteria are:

 

  1. qualification, experience and skills in providing Project advisory services for reviewing the hydrological studies of hydropower projects;
  2. a minimum of Post Graduate Degree in the relevant hydrological disciplines and must have at least 15 years of professional experience relevant to the assignment.
  3. description of similar assignments previously carried out - must have done at least two (2) similar assignments (hydrological of hydropower advisory services), and
  4. experience of working in Sub-Sahara Africa - at least one (1) of the assignments should be in Sub-Shara Africa - and other regions.

 

Evidence shall be attached as supporting documents for the Expression of Interest.

 

Objective

 

The Project is being prepared for seeking financial support of the World Bank (the “Bank”) and therefore must comply with the World Bank Safeguards Policies and Performance Standards (see the concept project information document stage at the WB website [1]).  Accordingly, the Mphanda Nkuwa Project needs to comply with the World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) – Community Health and Safety (ESS4[2]). To this effect two panel of experts (PoEs) need to be formed: (i) Panel of Experts for Dam Safety (PoE-DS); and (ii) Panel of Experts for Environmental and Social Management (PoE-ESM).

Key Responsibilities/ Scope of Reviews

 

The hydrologist will:

 

  1. Review of the hydrological studies pertaining to the long-term inflow to the reservoirs, and spillway and diversion design floods with reference to international criteria. Assess the adequacy of spillway and diversion facilities, also considering increasing hydrological variability associated with global warming. Review of soil erosion data and estimate of sediment yield into the reservoirs, estimated reservoir sedimentation, and assessment of the long-term sustainable capacity that could be maintained by implementing appropriate management strategies. Review of layouts related to sediment management of the reservoirs including sediment flushing.
  2. Review of the design of spillway and tailrace facilities including flow conditions, energy dissipation and need for hydraulic modelling.
  3. Review of the designs of the diversion works, schedule and risk factors associated with diversion during construction and with the closure of diversion works at initial reservoir filling.

 

Expected Assignment Timeline

 

The assignment is for a period of six (6) years, covering project preparation, construction, and initial reservoir filling. The initial contract will be signed for a period of 2 years, with the potential for an extension to cover the full duration of preparation and implementation. The contract will be time-based, with an annual ceiling of 20 working days, subject to extension if needed.
